strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined task: multiview, object-level change detection with viewpoint variation is a genuine gap; the paper convincingly argues that existing benchmarks either fix viewpoints or provide only semantic labels, and Table 1 situates SceneDiff against prior datasets fairly.

Substantial dataset contribution: 350 real-world video pairs (200 collected + 150 from HD-Epic), 1009 annotated changed objects with full instance masks, object attributes (size, deformability, change type), and a carefully designed SAM2-based annotation pipeline that reduces annotation cost (~5 min/pair). The annotation tool and protocol are documented in the supplement with a worked evaluation example (Fig. 20).

Sensible dual evaluation protocol (per-view and per-scene AP, plus type-aware APtype) that disentangles detection from change-type classification and can accommodate methods outputting masks, boxes, or points.

Training-free method is well engineered: joint π3 geometry regression, co-visibility-based frame pairing, asymmetric depth-difference reasoning to separate true changes from occlusion, DINO feature comparison, and region-based matching aggregated into a unified score, followed by 3D-consistent instance association. The pipeline is clearly described with equations and justified design decisions.

Strong empirical evidence: large improvements on the proposed benchmark (49.6/46.3 AP on SD-V vs. baselines) and on the external RC-3D benchmark (68.7 vs. 50.0 with sensor depth), plus additional comparisons on ChangeSim. Thorough ablations over geometry backbones (π3 vs. VGGT vs. FASt3R), appearance features, and score components, including insightful analysis of why π3 is more robust to changes than VGGT (supp. Sec. 7.5).

Honest and detailed limitations: ambiguity of object swaps, reliance on pretrained geometry models, failure analysis for cluttered repetitive scenes and limited-overlap reconstruction (with dataset statistics of how often failures occur), and explicit exclusion of semantic state changes.
End-to-end robotic demonstration (tidying robot) shows the task and method have practical downstream value, and dynamic-content experiments probe robustness beyond the curated benchmark.

Baseline treatment is generally careful and transparent: the authors attempt to give 3DGS-CD a fair shot (3 FPS splatting, their better-estimated poses, replacing the faulty occupancy grid, with analysis in supp.), and they feed π3 depth to CYWS-3D and describe an adjusted evaluation for CYWS-3D's paired predictions.
weaknesses: The method is primarily a composition of existing foundation models (π3, SAM, DINOv3) with hand-tuned heuristics and thresholds (λg=1.0, λf=0.5, λr=0.2, τsim=0.7, σmerge=1.4, etc.). While effective and well justified, there is limited algorithmic novelty, and several hyperparameters are set from the validation set of the authors' own benchmark, which could favor the method's fit to its own data.

The evaluation protocol contains design choices that plausibly favor the authors' pipeline: point-based matching from mask centroids, allowance of up to two detections per ground truth without penalty, and manual matching of VLM text outputs to labels. These are documented, but their sensitivity is not analyzed, and the protocol was co-designed with the method by the same authors.

Baseline performance on the new benchmark is extremely low (3DGS-CD: 2.0 AP; VLM: ~1.0 AP), making the headline relative improvements (84%, 37.4%) less meaningful; the comparison could be more informative with a stronger multiview-adapted baseline (e.g., correspondence-based detection using DINOv2 [20] or zero-shot scene change detection [6], which are cited but not compared).

Absolute performance remains modest, particularly on SD-K (per-scene AP 20.9, APtype 12.2) in cluttered egocentric kitchens; while the authors acknowledge the task is far from solved, the benchmark may be too hard/narrow for baselines, limiting its immediate utility as a comparative tool.

Annotation quality is not quantified: SAM2-propagated masks may contain systematic errors, and there is no inter-annotator agreement study or verification metric for the 350 pairs (only a review step described).

Dataset scale and diversity are moderate (50 scenes, 20 categories, predominantly indoor daily scenes; SD-K inherits HD-Epic's biases). Half the pairs are derived from one external source, which reduces independence between the two subsets.
Code, data, and the annotation tool are 'released upon acceptance'; reproducibility currently rests on the supplement's descriptions rather than verifiable artifacts.

The per-view vs. per-scene distinction for 'Moved' objects introduces ambiguity in AP vs. APtype (moved objects counted as separate instances for AP), which is reasonable but adds protocol complexity that other groups may interpret differently; a reference implementation is needed to ensure consistent evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing change-detection benchmarks either assume near-duplicate viewpoints or lack instance-level, per-scene multiview annotations. The proposed SceneDiff Benchmark (350 video pairs, ~1009 annotated objects with instance masks, change types, and attributes) is a meaningful and reusable resource for the community.

The training-free method is well motivated: aligning before/after sequences in 3D with a feed-forward geometry model (π3), then scoring changes at the region level using asymmetric depth-reprojection cues plus DINO features, is a sensible and clearly described design that addresses the viewpoint-variation confound.

The evaluation protocol is unusually detailed and thoughtfully designed (per-view vs per-scene AP, type-aware AP, point-based matching to accommodate different output formats, tolerance rules for segmentation granularity), with a worked visualization example in the supplement.

Experiments cover two-view (RC-3D, ChangeSim) and multiview settings, include VLM and 3DGS-CD baselines with documented adaptation effort, and contain substantial ablations over geometry models, feature extractors, and score-cue combinations, plus honest failure-mode analysis (repetitive clutter, reconstruction failure, lighting changes).

The robot tidying demonstration and the geometry-model robustness analysis (Fig. 15) add value beyond a simple leaderboard, and limitations are candidly discussed (ambiguity of swaps, reliance on pretrained models, scope to spatial changes).
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a concern. The 3DGS-CD baseline achieves only ~2.0 AP, and the VLM baseline near zero; despite the authors' documented adaptations, the large reported margins (84%, 37.4% relative AP) may partly reflect baselines operating far outside their intended regime rather than a fundamental advance. The comparison to CYWS-3D is the most informative, but that method cannot do cross-view association by design.

The method is a training-free pipeline combining π3, SAM, and DINOv3 with many hand-set components and hyperparameters (asymmetric visibility rules, three score weights, thresholding, merging procedure, status classification threshold). While ablations cover the cues and thresholds, the pipeline's complexity and brittleness to each modeling choice (e.g., SAM mask quality causing misalignment with GT, acknowledged in Fig. 7) is not fully quantified.

The SD-K subset is derived from HD-Epic where changes 'naturally occur' during cooking. Since the changed objects must be identified post-hoc by annotators, there is a risk of systematically missing unnoticed changes (silent false negatives in ground truth), and no inter-annotator agreement or annotation-quality audit is reported. The manually collected subset also follows collection guidelines (smooth trajectories, similar coverage) that may implicitly favor geometry-alignment-based approaches like the authors' own.

No learning-based or fine-tuned baselines are evaluated on the new benchmark; the benchmark is presented as a training/evaluation resource, yet all reported methods are training-free or zero-shot, leaving the benchmark's usefulness for supervised approaches untested.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code and data are promised only upon acceptance, the annotation protocol (human labels propagated with SAM2) is not independently verifiable, and the method depends on third-party foundation models whose availability/licensing could change.

Absolute performance remains low on the harder subset (per-scene APtype of 12.2 on SD-K), which supports the claim that the task is open but also means the benchmark's difficulty calibration and the practical significance of the improvements are hard to judge.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned benchmark contribution: SceneDiff Benchmark fills a genuine gap — prior multiview change detection datasets either lack instance-level object annotations (VL-CMU-CD, 3DGS-CD, PASLCD) or contain only one changed object per pair (RC-3D). 350 diverse real-world video pairs with dense instance masks, change types, and object attributes is a substantial and useful resource, and the accompanying annotation tooling and evaluation protocol (per-view and per-scene AP, AP_type) is well designed and thoroughly documented (Supp. Sec. 8.1).

The proposed training-free method is technically sound and clearly described: the asymmetric depth-difference cue (Eq. 1) to separate real changes from viewpoint-dependent occlusions is a sensible insight, and the combination of geometry reprojection, DINO-based appearance comparison, and region-based matching (Eqs. 2-4) is well justified by the ablations, which show E_feat dominates while geometry is essential as the alignment substrate.

Comprehensive and largely fair empirical evaluation: strong improvements on both the new benchmark (e.g., 49.6 vs 26.9 per-view AP on SD-V) and the established RC-3D two-view benchmark (68.7 vs 50.0 AP50), plus ChangeSim. Baselines include adapted CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD (with best-effort tuning detailed in Supp.), and VLM pipelines with careful prompt engineering and localization handling.

Thorough ablations and analysis: comparisons across geometry backbones (π3, VGGT, FASt3R), feature extractors (DINOv1/v2/v3), feature-cue combinations, and threshold sensitivity analyses; the supplement's failure-mode taxonomy (repetitive-item clutter, geometry failure, lighting changes) and geometry-robustness stress tests (Fig. 15) are unusually candid and useful for future work.

Demonstrated practical relevance through a real robot tidying application, including coordinate alignment between regressed geometry and a RealSense depth camera, adding credibility beyond benchmark numbers.
The limitations discussion (ambiguous swaps, reliance on pretrained reconstruction quality, scope limited to spatial changes) is meaningful and substantive rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the method is a training-free pipeline that composes existing foundation models (π3, DINOv3, SAM) with reprojected-depth and feature-similarity heuristics plus several hand-tuned constants (λg=1.0, λf=0.5, λr=0.2, τocc=-0.02, σmerge=1.4, τsim=0.7). This is defensible for a benchmark-centric contribution, but the algorithmic contribution is incremental and its hyperparameter sensitivity, while partially addressed (Figs. 17-18), is not exhaustively characterized.

Absolute performance of the proposed method remains modest (per-scene AP_type of 25.5 on SD-V, 12.2 on SD-K), and the benchmark's difficulty means the new dataset may be too hard for meaningful near-term progress on the Kitchen subset; the authors acknowledge this, but it tempers the immediate utility of the benchmark.

Potential baseline unfairness on the new benchmark: 3DGS-CD scores near zero (2.0/0.1 AP), making relative improvement claims (84%) less informative than the absolute comparison to CYWS-3D would suggest; although the authors provide detailed adaptation and analysis (Supp. Secs. 8.5, Fig. 22), rendering-based methods may simply be outside their regime on this data.

Benchmark scale and provenance concerns: 1009 annotated objects over 250 test pairs is still modest, 150 of 350 pairs derive from HD-Epic (cooking scenes only, which may narrow diversity), and self-collected data with crowd-style guidelines risks distribution bias toward easy, cooperative captures; annotation quality relies on SAM2 mask propagation, and no inter-annotator agreement or label-noise quantification is reported.

Some evaluation protocol choices are non-standard and could affect comparability (allowing up to two detection points per ground truth without penalty; point-based matching of mask centroids to boxes), and the oracle-tolerant setup may inflate AP relative to stricter object-detection conventions.

Computational cost is high relative to baselines (159.4s per sequence pair, mostly SAM masking, vs 23.9-30.5s), which limits practicality for the robotics applications the paper motivates; a runtime/performance trade-off analysis is absent from the main paper.

Reproducibility is currently conditional: code, data, and the annotation tool are promised for release only upon acceptance, and thresholds/hyperparameters are spread across the text; full release will be essential to realize the benchmark's value.

strengths: The SceneDiff Benchmark is a genuine and well-motivated contribution: it is the first multiview, instance-level change detection dataset with cross-view consistent IDs, 350 real-world video pairs from 50 scenes with 6K annotated frames and 1009 objects, clearly filling a gap relative to prior benchmarks (RC-3D, 3DGS-CD, PASLCD) as documented in Table 1.

The paper introduces a sensible three-tier evaluation protocol (px/im IoU, obj/im AP, obj/sc AP), with the scene-level metric directly addressing cross-view instance consistency, which is the practically relevant question. Supplemental change-type-aware evaluation further strengthens the protocol.

The method is clearly motivated: co-registering before/after sequences with a feed-forward 3D model, then detecting object-level geometric/appearance inconsistencies. The asymmetric depth-difference rule (Eq. 1) is a thoughtful treatment of the occlusion ambiguity problem.

Training-free design built on pretrained models (π3, SAM, DINOv3) is well-validated through ablations over backbone geometry models and feature extractors (Table 5), and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses in the supplement demonstrate robustness.
Evaluation breadth is a strength: results on the new benchmark, RC-3D (+30.6% relative AP), ChangeSim, and PASLCD, plus a closed-loop robotic tidying demonstration that shows practical utility.

The supplement is unusually thorough and honest: baseline adaptation details, failure analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, geometry failure, lighting changes), dynamic-content robustness, geometry model behavior under change, and inference times. The limitations section is substantive and specific.
Reproducibility is addressed: codebase attached, dataset, annotation tool, and evaluation code promised for release, and annotation effort/collection guidelines are documented.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: SceneDiff is an assembly of pretrained models (π3, SAM, DINOv3) with hand-designed scoring, thresholding, and merging steps; most design decisions (weights, thresholds) were tuned on the authors' own benchmark validation set, raising a concern that the method co-evolved with the benchmark it evaluates on.

Dataset collection has potential biases: 200 of 350 pairs were collected by 7 team members following guidelines that avoid hard conditions (smooth camera only, no moving objects/people, avoid low light implicitly, prefer similar coverage). SD-V skews toward larger objects, and the dataset is modest in scale (1009 objects), which may limit the task difficulty it captures compared to real deployment scenarios.

Fairness of some baseline comparisons requires care: the authors use their own regressed poses as input to 3DGS baselines, disable 3DGS-CD's occupancy grid, and apply custom SAM-based adaptations for CYWS and MV3DCD. These choices are documented and partly justified (e.g., supplementary box-level vs mask-level checks), and they also evaluate on PASLCD where 3DGS baselines are at home, but the headroom for baseline mistreatment on the new benchmark cannot be fully excluded.

Absolute performance on the headline obj/sc AP metric is low (22.8 SD-V, 10.6 SD-K), indicating the task is far from solved; the '53.0% relative improvement' abstract claim averages two metrics on the authors' own benchmark and somewhat overstates the headline contribution.

The VLM baseline evaluation relies on manual text-to-GT matching and SAM3 confidence as detection score, making that comparison difficult to interpret as a statement about VLM capability on this task.

Runtime is notable: ~159s per sequence pair, dominated by SAM masking, which could limit the practical robotic applications the paper advertises; running-time comparison with 3DGS baselines is fair but the method itself is not lightweight.
There is no explicit societal-impact statement (privacy of collected household videos, dual-use considerations), though data collection guidelines mention avoiding identity information.

strengths: Strong Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: the paper introduces the first multiview change detection benchmark with dense cross-view consistent instance-level annotations (350 video pairs, ~1009 annotated objects, 6K annotated frames across indoor/outdoor real scenes, including egocentric footage from HD-Epic). Table 1 clearly situates it against prior datasets, which are mostly semantic-label, similar-viewpoint, or very small (5-100 pairs).

Practical annotation infrastructure: the SAM2-based annotation tool with prompt propagation and review interface (reducing annotation time from ~30 to ~10 minutes per pair), plus documented collection guidelines and split design (validation/test separated by physical scene), supports reproducibility and future extension of the dataset.

The proposed obj/sc AP metric meaningfully extends existing per-view change detection evaluation to cross-view instance consistency, which is arguably the metric that matters for downstream applications; a stricter change-type-aware variant is also provided in the supplement.

The training-free method is well-motivated and clearly presented: co-registering before/after sequences with a feed-forward geometry model (π3), an asymmetric depth-difference rule that disambiguates true changes from occlusion, DINOv3-based appearance reprojection, region-level matching, and 3D voxelized score aggregation for instance association. Each component is justified and ablated (Tab. 5).

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: comparisons on four external datasets (RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim, plus the new benchmark), ablations over three geometry backbones and three feature extractors, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, failure-mode analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, geometry failure, lighting), and a closed-loop robotic tidying demonstration that evidences practical utility.

Baseline treatment is documented in detail in the supplement (finetuning protocol for CYWS-2D, providing π3 depth to CYWS-3D, adapting 3DGS-CD/MV3DCD with regressed poses and denser sampling), and SAM-based box-to-mask conversion is verified not to degrade baselines (Sec. 8.6/8.7), which mitigates some fairness concerns.

The limitations section is substantive rather than token: ambiguity of swaps, dependence on pose quality under low light/textureless/sparse views, and the restriction to spatial (not semantic-state) changes are honestly identified, with a dedicated failure-case analysis in the supplement.
weaknesses: Headline relative improvements (53.0% and 30.6%) should be interpreted cautiously: they are computed against baselines that are demonstrably mismatched to the setting. The 3DGS-based methods fail mainly because SceneDiff's trajectories require view extrapolation rather than interpolation (acknowledged in Sec. 8.4), and the VLM baseline shows severe recognition/localization bottlenecks (113/369 correct names in SD-V). Absolute performance is low (obj/sc AP of 22.8 on SD-V and 10.6 on SD-K), indicating the task remains far from solved and the margins partly reflect baseline unsuitability.

Potential evaluation circularity: ground-truth masks are produced by SAM2-based annotation, and the method itself (and the mask-based AP conversion for baselines) relies on SAM masks. This could systematically favor SAM-style region decomposition and should be analyzed (e.g., agreement between human corrections and SAM output, or a subset of fully manual annotations).

Method hyperparameters (feature weights, thresholds, merge thresholds) are tuned on the SceneDiff validation set; while the authors report the same parameters across all benchmarks and show low sensitivity, the claim of strong cross-domain generalization (RC-3D, PASLCD) would be cleaner with a fully zero-touch parameter policy stated explicitly per benchmark.

The method is slow in practice: 159.4s per sequence pair, dominated by SAM mask generation (~4s per image). This is far better than >30min for 3DGS baselines, but limits applicability for the robotic/inventory scenarios motivated in the introduction without further engineering.

The MV3DCD adaptation on SceneDiff (60% region-ratio threshold, no occupancy grid) involves nontrivial design decisions by the authors that could disadvantage that baseline; the counterbalancing PASLCD result (only +1.2 mIoU over MV3DCD, losing on several scenes) suggests the method's advantage narrows considerably under baselines' favorable, densely-captured conditions.

Dataset scale is modest by modern standards (350 pairs, 1009 objects from 50 scenes collected largely by 7 people), and the SD-K subset inherits HD-Epic's Cooking-oriented changes, which may include deformable/semantic state changes that sit awkwardly with the purely spatial change-type taxonomy the method is designed for.

Several algorithmic choices receive limited justification: the fixed score weights (λ=1.0/0.5/0.1), the merging threshold σmerge=1.4 for a summed feature+geometry score, and greedy one-to-one object matching with τsim=0.7 are validated only empirically; a formal analysis of the asymmetric depth rule's failure under occlusion errors is absent (Eq. 1's τocc=-0.02 is scale-dependent on the unit-cube normalization, which deserves discussion).

Reproducibility of the dataset is currently promised rather than demonstrated (release upon acceptance for anonymity); given the contribution is primarily a benchmark, the strength of the submission is contingent on that release.

strengths: The SceneDiff Benchmark addresses a genuine gap: it is the first multiview, instance-level change detection dataset with cross-view consistent object IDs, diverse real-world indoor/outdoor scenes (350 pairs, 1009 annotated objects), and a SAM2-assisted annotation pipeline that reduced annotation cost substantially. The design and curation effort (160h collection, 60h annotation) is significant, and the release of the dataset, tool, and code maximizes community value.

The training-free SceneDiff algorithm is well-motivated and technically sound: co-registering before/after sequences with feed-forward 3D models (π³), asymmetric depth-reprojection rules that disambiguate real changes from occlusions, and region-level aggregation over SAM masks are sensible, clearly explained design choices. The metric suite (px/im IoU, obj/im AP, obj/sc AP) is well constructed, with obj/sc AP correctly identified as the most practically meaningful metric.

Experimental evidence is comprehensive and unusually careful for a benchmark paper: results on the proposed benchmark, RC-3D (30.6% relative AP gain), PASLCD, and ChangeSim; ablations over geometry models and feature extractors; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; explicit failure analysis (cluttered repetitive scenes, geometry failure, lighting changes); and a change-type-aware stricter metric. The supplementary treatment of baseline adaptations (CYWS-2D/3D, 3DGS-CD, MV3DCD, VLM) is thorough and transparent, including sanity checks showing SAM mask conversion does not disadvantage baselines.

The closed-loop robotic tidying application demonstrates real-world utility beyond benchmark numbers, and the limitations section is honest and substantive (ambiguous configurations, pose-estimation failures, semantic state changes out of scope).
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains low, especially on obj/sc AP (22.8 on SD-V, 10.6 on SD-K) and on the cluttered SD-K subset, and the claimed 53.0% relative improvement should be read against this context. The task is shown to be far from solved, which limits the benchmark's near-term discriminative power between stronger methods (though this also motivates the dataset).

The method's dependence on multiple specific pretrained models (π³, SAM, DINOv3) makes results tied to the current foundation-model stack; while the ablations show robustness across backbones and the training-free framing is a stated design choice, the contribution is more of an integration/system than a new algorithmic insight, and future model shifts may change the rankings. Inference time (159.4s per sequence pair, dominated by SAM masking) is also comparatively heavy.

The dataset, while the largest of its kind, is modest in scale (350 pairs, 1009 objects) and partly self-collected by 7 people; the SD-K subset is derived from HD-Epic under a license whose redistribution terms deserve explicit statement. The 'moved' labeling convention (e.g., a moved object vs. separate removed+added pair) introduces a judgment call the annotation guidelines mitigate but do not eliminate.

Several key details are deferred to the supplement (baseline implementation choices, dynamic-content handling requiring manual masks, full PASLCD results), so the main paper alone understates the caveats around baseline comparisons; some comparisons (e.g., 3DGS methods under large viewpoint changes) involve adapted evaluation setups that, while well-justified, are not fully standardized.
